title: Keep food clean
summary: Keeping food clean with little water: wash your hands with soap before you touch food. Keep raw meat, poultry, seafood and eggs apart from food that won’t be cooked. Wash dishes, counters and cutting boards, sanitize them with the food mix and let them air dry, by the steps in Clean and disinfect, using safe water. Anyone who has had vomiting or diarrhea prepares no food until at least 2 days after it stops.
doFirst: Wash your hands with soap and the cleanest water you have before, during and after preparing food, and before eating (CDC, FoodSafety.gov). How, with little water: Washing hands with little water.

Anyone who has had vomiting or diarrhea must not prepare or handle food, handle the group’s water, or care for others. CDC: “Wait at least 2 days (48 hours) after symptoms stop.” Wait 3 days (72 hours) if the group can manage it (Minnesota Department of Health; University of Minnesota Extension).
Keep raw meat, poultry, seafood and eggs apart from food that won’t be cooked: separate cutting boards, plates and utensils (FoodSafety.gov).
Wash dishes, counters and cutting boards, sanitize them with the food mix and let them air dry, by the steps in Clean and disinfect.
Safe water for drinking, cooking and washing yourself is bottled, boiled or treated water (CDC). How to make it: Make water safe.

blocks.p: Wash with soap and water (FoodSafety.gov, CDC):

list: Before, during and after preparing food.
After handling raw meat, poultry, seafood or their juices, or uncooked eggs.
Before eating, and before feeding children.
After using the toilet, changing diapers or cleaning up a child who has used the toilet.
After touching garbage or an animal, and before and after caring for someone who is sick.
Before preparing food, wash with boiled (then cooled) water, bottled water, or water from another acceptable source (New York State Department of Health).
Anyone preparing food must wash with soap and water; sanitizer does not replace it for them (CDC, evacuation centers).
Don’t touch ready-to-eat food with bare hands; use utensils (University of Minnesota Extension).
Use one cutting board for fresh produce and other food that won’t be cooked before it is eaten, and another for raw meat, poultry or seafood. Replace boards when they are worn (FoodSafety.gov).
Use separate plates and utensils for cooked and raw food (FoodSafety.gov).
Keep raw meat, poultry and seafood in containers or sealed, leakproof plastic bags (FoodSafety.gov).
Wash plates, utensils and cutting boards that touched raw meat, poultry, seafood, eggs or flour (FoodSafety.gov), then sanitize them as in Clean and disinfect.
Don’t wash raw meat, poultry, eggs or seafood: it spreads germs around the kitchen (FoodSafety.gov).
Rinse fruit and vegetables under running water before you peel or cut them, without soap, bleach or produce washes, and scrub firm produce with a clean brush (FoodSafety.gov). Use safe water (CDC).
Keep food in covered containers. Keep cooking and eating utensils clean (Ready.gov).

blocks.p: Cooking temperatures, and how long cooked food can wait, are in Cook without power and Is it still good?

sections.h: Dishes and surfaces with little water

list: Use disposable plates, cups and cutlery if you have them (CDC).
Scrape leftover food off into the garbage before you wash (University of Florida IFAS Extension).
Wash, rinse, sanitize with the food mix, and air dry: the steps and the mix are in Clean and disinfect, under Dishes with little water and Surfaces.
No hot water? Cold water is fine, but the sanitizing step matters even more (University of Florida IFAS Extension).
When the wash or rinse water gets dirty, empty the basin, clean it and refill it (University of Florida IFAS Extension).
Wash dish cloths often (FoodSafety.gov).

blocks.p: Where to pour the dirty water: Garbage and dirty water. What to heat water on with the power out: Cook without power.
Pans, dishes, utensils and counters that flood water touched, and pots and pans that fire-fighting chemicals touched, have their own steps in Is it still good?

blocks.warn: Anyone who has had vomiting or diarrhea must not prepare or handle food, handle the group’s water, or care for others. CDC: “Wait at least 2 days (48 hours) after symptoms stop.” Wait 3 days (72 hours) if the group can manage it (Minnesota Department of Health; University of Minnesota Extension).

list: Wash dishes and food surfaces, then sanitize them with bleach (see Clean and disinfect).
Throw away food and food packaging within 25 feet (7.6 m) of the vomit or stool (University of Minnesota Extension).

blocks.p: Bottles and baby feeding items have their own cleaning steps.
